title: Lotus Improv (1991-1996): the cube spreadsheet — dimensions first, cells last
summary: Lotus Improv was a spreadsheet rebuilt from first principles: instead of a flat grid of cells holding data, formulas and notes, Improv separated the concepts. Data lived in named multidimensional categories (e.g. Region, Month, Product); formulas lived outside the cells and referenced names, never A1 addresses; the grid was only an input/output view you could pivot with one click (regional sales by month becomes monthly sales by region). In-memory OLAP cubes, named ranges, and plain-language formulas on a desktop in 1991.
mechanism: The ahead-of-its-time mechanism was the dimension-first model: a model is a set of dimensions with members, formulas attach to dimension members (profit = revenue - expense for every month, every region, at once), and views are projections. This made models structurally resistant to the two classic spreadsheet sins — broken cell references and copy-pasted formula drift — because there were no cell addresses to break. LotusScript (its embedded scripting language) let models grow into custom applications.
decline: Development was put on hiatus in 1994 after slow Windows sales and officially killed in April 1996 after IBM bought Lotus. Post-mortems cite a corporate immune response (Lotus's own 1-2-3 sales teams wouldn't sell it), marketing that framed it as '1-2-3 done right' instead of the OLAP tool it was, Excel being Office-bundled at marginal cost, users needing to unlearn the grid, and in-memory cubes that couldn't page to disk on 1990s hardware. Guess flag: internal sales deliberations are reconstructed from retrospective accounts, not Lotus memos.
revival_recipe: Take the dimension-first model, not the product: named dimensions, formulas on members instead of cells, and views as projections. Modern hardware removes the in-memory-cube limit that strangled Improv; plain dicts do the work. Build it as a small stdlib engine with no grid UI at all — slices, dices, and named formulas — and let the giant rectangle-war stay in the past.
levi_application: core/levi/cube/: Cube — a tiny stdlib multidimensional pivot engine: named dimensions with members, named formulas over member tuples, slice/dice/project views, JSON persistence. Honest use: LEVI's own analytics (demand-signal aggregation across time/source/topic) without reaching for pandas or a paid BI tool. Built and committed 2026-09-23 under standing approval.
skepticism: Do not romanticize: Improv was genuinely harder to learn than Excel, and Joel Spolsky's critique has teeth — it was aimed at a specific market and lost the generality war. The claim here is narrower: the dimension-first model is load-bearing for analysis, not that Improv would have won.

title: HyperCard (1987-2004): the shipped-free stack anyone could program
summary: Bill Atkinson's HyperCard shipped free with every Macintosh for seventeen years: a visual hypermedia system of stacks, cards, backgrounds, fields and buttons, with HyperTalk, an English-like scripting language ('go to next card', 'put field "Name" into x'). Schoolteachers, doctors and children built working software; the best-selling PC game of the 1990s, Myst, was built in it; Brendan Eich cited HyperTalk as an inspiration for JavaScript; Ward Cunningham traced the wiki to a stack he wrote in the late 1980s.
mechanism: The load-bearing mechanism was the erased boundary between tool and artifact: the authoring environment and the running stack were the same thing — browse a card, flip a switch, and you are editing it. Objects (buttons, fields) carried their scripts with them; cards were addressable, linkable documents years before the web. Distribution was trivial: hand someone a stack file and they could run AND modify it. No build step, no toolchain, no app-store review.
decline: Moved to Claris (which charged for authoring), never got color or networking in time, and was left to wither: the HyperCard 3.0 rewrite (color, internet, in-browser stacks) demoed through the late 1990s but was stalled when QuickTime's team was redirected, and Steve Jobs reassigned the team in 2000 — Atkinson said it had 'Sculley's stink' on it. Apple kept selling 2.x unchanged until March 2004, never ported it to OS X. The tool that inspired the Web died, in part, because it never connected to the Web. Guess flag: exact internal politics are reconstructed from participant accounts.
revival_recipe: Take the stack metaphor and the tool-is-the-artifact boundary-erasure, not the product: a local-first 'stack' primitive where documents are live objects you can script in place with readable language, and stacks are plain files you can hand to anyone. Clean-room: no HyperTalk, no Mac ROM calls — LEVI's own card/stack objects over JSON, with a small readable event-scripting layer in LEVI's own form.
levi_application: Queued in build queue 2026-09-23: a native stack-authoring primitive for LEVI (cards as live scriptable documents, stacks as portable files) — the honest ADDITION is end-user programmability for LEVI's own surfaces (desk, canvas), not a HyperCard clone. Larger build; queued, not half-built.
skepticism: Do not romanticize: 1-bit black-and-white stacks were a hard ceiling, performance was poor, and real databases outgrew it fast. The living idea is end-user programmability with zero toolchain, not the 1987 feature set.

title: Palm HotSync (1996-2009): the one-button honest local sync the cloud killed
era: 1996–2009 (Palm OS; Mac support cut in OS X 10.6 Snow Leopard)
summary: Press one button on the Palm cradle and every app on the device synced with the desktop over a local cable: contacts, calendar, notes, third-party databases — via an open conduit plugin API any developer could target. Your computer was the server. No account, no cloud intermediary, no subscription, no telemetry; sync worked in a bunker with no internet at all.
mechanism: The load-bearing mechanism was the conduit contract: the sync engine was a dumb transport plus a registry, and every data type supplied its own conduit — a small plugin implementing compare/export/import for that app's records. Sync was an explicit user-initiated act (press the cradle button), ran entirely over a local serial/USB link, and the desktop copy and device copy were peers with a visible sync log. No intermediary ever held the data; privacy was architectural, not a policy.
decline: Killed by the smartphone/cloud era: Palm moved to webOS, Apple dropped the HotSync conduit from Snow Leopard in 2009, and the industry re-centralized sync through Google/Microsoft/Apple accounts — a business choice, not a technical necessity. The capability PalmOS users still cite as missing on iOS/Android is exactly this: local-only sync with no internet intermediary. Guess flag: exact market-share causality is inferred; Palm's decline had many parents.
revival_recipe: Take the conduit contract, not the cradle: a local-first sync protocol where each data type registers a conduit (export/import/merge functions), sync is an explicit user-initiated act over a local transport, conflicts resolve with a visible log instead of silent cloud merges, and no third party ever sees the data. stdlib sockets or files; no accounts.
levi_application: Queued in build queue 2026-09-23: core/levi/conduit/ — an honest local sync layer for LEVI (device ↔ his machines): conduit registration, one-command sync, conflict ledger, zero cloud. The ADDITION is user-owned synchronization as a native capability; LEVI already has backup/, conduit/ would be its sync twin.
skepticism: Do not romanticize: HotSync was slow, conduit conflicts could duplicate records, and Palm Desktop's UI was dated. The honest core is the local-first sync contract and the explicit user-initiated act — not the cradle.

title: Borland Sidekick (1984-1999): the resident utilities that never made you leave
summary: Borland Sidekick was a terminate-and-stay-resident (TSR) personal information manager: press Ctrl-Alt from inside ANY running program and a window popped up with a calendar, notepad, calculator, address book and dialer — then you dismissed it and your program was exactly where you left it. $49.95 in 1984; over a million copies in the first three years. It anticipated the windowed UI and the always-available assistant by a decade.
mechanism: The load-bearing mechanism was ambient residency with hotkey invocation: the tools lived in memory beside your work, reachable in one gesture, requiring no context switch, no app launch, no alt-tab archaeology. The notepad could copy text straight off the screen beneath it. Later versions (2.0) used the Paradox engine with open file formats, and the Time Planner could reconcile two schedule files across a LAN — early peer sync.
decline: The TSR trick died when protected-mode multitasking (Windows 95) made resident popups unnecessary — and then the idea was re-absorbed into the OS tray, widgets, and eventually the phone's notification shade, where it serves the platform's engagement goals instead of the user's. Starfish sold to Motorola in 1998 for $325M; Nokia discontinued Sidekick 99, the last version. Guess flag: acquisition figures come from retrospective reporting.
revival_recipe: Take ambient residency, not the TSR hack: a small always-on local panel of tools (scratch note, calculator, quick capture, unit conversion) invoked by one hotkey from anywhere, storing everything locally in plain files, never phoning home. On modern systems this is a tray/menu-bar resident or a terminal multiplexer pane — the hard part was never technical, it was refusing to rent the slot to engagement bait.
levi_application: Archived as inspiration 2026-09-23. The ADDITION direction is a resident quick-capture layer for LEVI's daemon (one-keystroke capture → local inbox → archive), which LEVI's quickdial/ and daemon/ partly cover; held as inspiration rather than a new module to avoid duplicating existing ground.
skepticism: Do not romanticize: TSRs were fragile memory hacks that crashed machines, and Sidekick's later versions bloated. The living idea is one-gesture ambient tools with zero context switch — not DOS memory residency.
